extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and students, especially public affairs and government-relations specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, targeting, executing, and evaluating public affairs (government relations and activist-publics) programs, including how to identify types of publics, how to influence officials, program models, and evaluation criteria. Draws on situational theory of publics and empirical studies to recommend objectives and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate responsibility issue classification (primary/secondary/tertiary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify corporate social responsibility issues according to primary (basic economic functions), secondary (consequences of those functions), and tertiary (general social problems). Examples given: primary—quality of products and services, corporate profits; secondary—pollution, inflation, monopoly, human relations on the job, employment of minorities; tertiary—decay of the cities, quality of education, support of charitable organizations, unemployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to map issues to publics and to decide which responsibilities the corporation should address or communicate about. Statistical analysis of these issue-types helps identify publics and their likely concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aware public (characteristics and communication implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large aware public that has high involvement and problem recognition mostly for secondary responsibilities and high constraint recognition—believing it could do little to resolve the problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This public is potential activist but not necessarily a constituent public. Important for communications about how the corporation has corrected consequences of its behavior because constrained publics frequently turn to government for help. Communications should focus on corrective actions and ways to reduce perceived constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activist public (characteristics and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: An activist public with high involvement and problem recognition about many issues and high constraint recognition; they frequently join pressure groups and work with government on social issues and believe business should address general social issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets for policy and advocacy communications. Likely to support interest groups and demand change from business as part of policy negotiations. Expect them to be politically active; communication should anticipate pressure-group behaviors and policy demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive public (characteristics and attention triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A passive public with low involvement and problem recognition on most issues except widely shared ones (pollution, product quality, inflation, education, human relations at work). This public may not feel constrained on issues it perceives involvement with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although generally passive, this public will become active on specific issues; public affairs specialists must monitor and pay attention when such issues arise and tailor communications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public types from multiple-issue analysis (activist, apathetic, single-issue publics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analysis across issues can produce multiple publics such as an activist public, an apathetic public, and several single-issue publics (e.g., steel/nuclear, Ford Pinto, Nestlé activist). Each has characteristic levels of problem recognition, involvement, constraint recognition, cognitions/attitudes, and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by situational-theory measures (problem recognition, involvement, constraint recognition) to predict communications behavior (message retention, attitude, behavior) and to choose appropriate tactics for each public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apathetic public (low-involvement/fatalistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public that is low-involvement and fatalistic on most issues and only moderately involved even on the most involving issue; it processes little information and rarely communicates or acts on issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect limited processing and behavior; design communications recognizing limited engagement—use highly salient, concise messages or rely on intermediaries to reach them on the single involving issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-issue public (constituent or interest-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics that are highly involved and problem-facing about one or two issues only (e.g., 'Steel/Nuclear' or 'Ford Pinto' publics). They may be composed of people who work in or have stakes in related industries and may act as constituent publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate only about the target issues; anticipate hedged cognitions (both pro- and antibusiness beliefs). These publics may be persuaded on specific policy positions but not necessarily moved on broad attitudes toward business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedging vs. wedging cognitions (message effects on publics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics often 'hedge' by holding both antibusiness and probusiness cognitions; public affairs programs can get publics to 'hedge' their antibusiness view with a probusiness view but cannot easily 'wedge out' antibusiness beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic communication objectives: aim for message retention and acceptance (hedging) rather than radical attitude replacement (wedging). Expect partial cognitive change rather than complete reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint recognition (influencing officials by placing constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: People (including government officials) who perceive external constraints have little need to communicate; one way to influence officials is to place constraints upon them so their behavior is determined by outside forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobilize legal and ethical pressures (e.g., threats to reelection through constituent mobilization, alliances with other influential groups) rather than illegal tactics (bribes). If constraints succeed, limited communication (only informing officials of constraints) may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate vs. constrain—two ways to influence government officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The governmental relations specialist can influence officials either by forcing/constraining them to act as desired or by communicating persuasively to negotiate or get votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer legal constraints rooted in political realities (reelection pressures) and use communication to persuade officials who are not constrained. Choose tactic based on the official's situational variables (involvement, problem recognition, constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target officials who communicate symmetrically and frequently
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials who communicate symmetrically (exchange information and accurately predict constituents' views) and frequently are better targets for communication; such officials are more likely to be re-elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and prioritize officials (and staff) who demonstrate symmetric communication patterns; they will be more receptive and effective channels for your messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement and home-district salience as targeting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators communicate most actively about issues that involve their home districts or states; involvement at home is a key predictor of active communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grassroots lobbying and constituent contacts to reach legislators on district-involving issues. Emphasize shared involvements and local impacts in messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem recognition and committee specialization for targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators specialize in certain issues—often those aligned with the committees on which they sit; House members can specialize more than Senators due to committee loads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map your issue to relevant congressional committees (foreign relations; environment, energy, national resources, agriculture; economic policy; domestic social policy; legal and judicial systems) and target representatives/staff accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of legislative staff and issue networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative personal and committee staff and representatives of interest groups form 'issue networks' that are crucial in Washington; staff often limit or shape information flowing to members and can be entrepreneurial in initiating policy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat staff as primary publics—cultivate relationships, provide concise usable information, and recognize staff influence on members' decisions. Use staff as entry points into committee decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive communication behavior—reaching passive officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials who do not specialize in an issue may be passive communicators and may vote based on the limited information they receive; all representatives can vote, so reaching passive officials can matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise, targeted information (personal contact, brief reports, constituent letters) or use active legislative publics to pass information to passive officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations objectives for programs (five objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five objectives for public relations programs (defined in Chapter 9): communication, message retention, message acceptance, effect on attitude, and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic objectives for public affairs programs—communication, message retention, and message acceptance are achievable and measurable; attitude and behavior change are harder to control and should be secondary objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methods for public affairs efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Common evaluation approaches: measures of audience response to communications (acceptance of views—attitude objective), results of lobbying efforts (passage, defeat, or modification of legislation—behavior objective), and financial/competitive impact (reduced costs, increased profits—often unrealistic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure communication contacts foremost (number and quality of contacts with officials). Use surveys and informal methods to assess message retention and acceptance among officials; be cautious about attributing financial outcomes directly to PR efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effectiveness ratings of government-relations activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners rated activities for effectiveness (serving as 'eyes and ears' 4.0; representing the company to regulatory agencies 3.4; influencing proposed legislation 3.3; influencing compliance with regulation 3.0 on a 1–5 scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize intelligence-gathering and representation roles; while lobbying and influencing regulation matter, practitioners often find the information-and-representation functions most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program models for activist publics and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Program models: two-way symmetric model is theoretically essential for activist publics. Anti-patterns: press agentry/publicity ('whitewash') often antagonizes activists; purely public-information approaches can fail if organizations don't provide the information publics want or omit disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt two-way engagement where possible; avoid whitewash publicity and one-sided 'spin.' Provide balanced information, listen to activist concerns, and institutionalize appropriate programs (consumer relations, environmental relations, minority/community/urban relations) rather than treating issues solely as media/employee problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coorientation and candid communication about advantages/disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Coorientation (comparing what publics think you think and what you actually think) reveals mismatches—e.g., the public recognizes both advantages and disadvantages of a project while the organization appears to see only advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coorientation methods to detect perceptual gaps and communicate both advantages and disadvantages candidly to avoid being seen as myopic. Example: Army Corps of Engineers—failure to disclose disadvantages led to distrust.
